sentences.text: The holotype consists of five preserved cervical vertebrae identified as the fifth through ninth cervical vertebrae.
These bones possess hollow centers with a cortical bone layer approximately 1 mm thick.
The animal was covered with hair-like pycnofibers.
Fossils were found in 2000 by the Office Chérifien des Phosphates near Khouribga in central Morocco.
The specimen was designated the holotype for the new species Phosphatodraco mauritanicus in 2003.
It is debated whether azhdarchids like Phosphatodraco were skim-feeders in coastal waters or foraged terrestrially like storks.
Witton and Naish argued that azhdarchids likely inhabited inland environments because over half of their fossils come from fluvial or alluvial deposits.
Witton suggested in 2013 that azhdarchids could stride through vegetated areas with long limbs and downturned jaws to reach the ground.
Phosphatodraco is classified as a genus of azhdarchid pterosaur.
A 2018 phylogenetic analysis by Longrich and colleagues identified Phosphatodraco as an azhdarchid and the sister taxon of Aralazhdarcho from Kazakhstan.
In 2025, Pêgas and colleagues named the clade Phosphatodraconia to include Phosphatodraco, Aralazhdarcho, Eurazhdarcho, and Wellnhopterus.
Phosphatodraco lived during the Maastrichtian age of the Late Cretaceous in the Oulad Abdoun Phosphatic Basin near Khouribga, central Morocco.
It was one of the last pterosaurs to live just before the Cretaceous-Paleogene mass extinction ended the group.

There is a debate over the vertebral order of the holotype, with some researchers identifying them as C5–C9 and others as C3–C8. Kellner's reinterpretation proposed that the order of the vertebrae should be shifted to C3 through C8. The debate over vertebral order affects the estimated wingspan, which is considered to be either 5 meters or 4 meters depending on the interpretation.
